title.en: The Balche Vessels at the East of the God House
title.zh: 神屋東側的巴爾切酒槽

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II: Religion of the Lacandones

summary.en: Owing to the necessity of fermentation, the balche must be made before the day of the rite. A large supply of the bark of the tree is collected and placed in one of the hollow logs situated at the east of the sacred hut; in a second hollow log a quantity of honey, or sugar cane and water, is placed. The syrup is strained and poured into the log containing the balche bark, and the contents allowed to ferment — sometimes for not more than a single day.
summary.zh: 因須發酵，巴爾切酒須於祭日之前釀成。取大量巴爾切樹皮，置於神屋東側的掏空木槽之一；另一槽盛蜂蜜——或蔗糖加水。糖漿濾淨，傾入盛樹皮之槽，令其發酵——有時僅一日即成。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: Owing to the necessity of fermentation, the balche must be made before the day set for the rite to come off. A large supply of the bark of the tree is collected and placed in one of the hollow logs made for the purpose and situated at the east of the sacred hut. In the second hollow log a quantity of honey or, if this is lacking, a large supply of sugar cane together with water is placed.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: The sirup is then strained and poured into the log containing the balche bark. The log is left uncovered and the contents allowed to ferment, sometimes for not more than a single day. The early accounts speak of this custom of drinking large quantities of balche as most healthful, and that after the common use of it was prohibited by the Spaniards, the natives suffered in consequence.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Copal Before the Idols of the Encampment
title.zh: 營地諸神像前的柯巴脂

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: In the prayers given before the idols, the other and lesser deities are invoked to come and carry the sacrifices offered and present them to 'the great lord.' The two Plumeria flowers, red and white, the father and mother of Nohochakyum, are placed one of each kind on the mouth of the brasero containing his idol, and the copal is burned before the stones brought home from the shrines.
summary.zh: 在神像前的禱詞中，另呼諸小神前來承載所獻犧牲，呈於「偉大之主」。紅白兩色雞蛋花——諾霍查庫姆之父與母——各一朵置於盛其神像的香爐口上；柯巴脂即焚於自聖地迎回的石像之前。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: In the prayers given before the idols, the other and lesser deities are invoked to come and carry the sacrifices offered and present them to 'the great lord.' Two flowers, the red Plumeria and the white Plumeria, are considered the father and mother respectively of Nohochakyum; one of each kind is placed on the mouth of the brasero containing the idol of Nohochakyum.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Stones Carried Home from the Shrines of the Gods

region.zh: 恰帕斯烏蘇馬辛塔河諸聖地

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: Only those gods are represented in an encampment to whose shrine a pilgrimage has been made and a stone either carved or otherwise brought back. These journeys cannot be made at will, but only after the god has shown himself as willing to receive such a pilgrimage; the home of Ioananohqu in a high cliff on the western shore of Lake Petha was visited in company with some Indians who went there to burn copal and offer sacrifices.
summary.zh: 營地中僅有那些曾往其聖地朝拜、並將雕成或取回之石迎回家的神明。此行不可任意為之，唯神自允之後方可；佩塔湖西岸高崖上的伊奧阿諾赫居所，即曾由印第安人相偕前往焚柯巴脂、行獻祭之地。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: All the gods named in the previous list are not usually represented in any one encampment. Only those are found to whose shrine a pilgrimage has been made and a stone either carved or otherwise brought back. These journeys cannot be made at will, but only after the god has shown himself as willing to receive such a pilgrimage.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: In a high cliff on the western shore of Lake Petha there lives the god Ioananohqu, and on the opposite side of the lake the deity called Kakoch. The home of the former is the only one that has been located precisely, the abode of the god having been visited in company with some Indians who went there to burn copal and offer sacrifices.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Suhuy Kaq: The Virgin Fire and Healing
title.zh: 蘇胡伊·卡克：聖潔之火與醫愈

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Parts II-III

summary.en: The god named Kaq (fire) lives near Tenosique; among the early Mayas there was a goddess called Suhuy Kaq (virgin fire), and this Lacandon god may be connected with her, as new fire has to be made at certain points in the various rites. Suhuyqaq is the spirit of the new fire, a god of healing: at every rite the old flame is put out and fire is drawn fresh for the gods.
summary.zh: 名為卡克（火）的神居於特諾西克附近；古馬雅人中有一位名蘇胡伊·卡克（貞潔之火）的女神，此拉坎敦神或與之相承——因各種祭儀中的特定環節都必須生新火。蘇胡伊·卡克即新火之靈、醫愈之神：每逢祭禮，舊火熄滅，為神另取新焰。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: The god named Kaq (fire) lives near Tenosique. Among the early Mayas there was a goddess called Suhuy Kaq (virgin fire). This god of the Lacandones may be connected with her, as new fire has to be made at certain points in the various rites. Suhuyqaq is the spirit of the new fire, a god of healing.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Mensabak, the God Above the Rain Cloud
title.zh: 門薩巴克：雨雲之上的神

region.zh: 恰帕斯聖伊波利托附近

source.work: Alfred M. Tozzer, A Comparative Study of the Mayas and the Lacandones (1907), Part II

summary.en: Mensabak lives near San Hipolito; he is probably identified as the god of rain. He is also called Yumkanasabak — the god who is above the rain cloud — and this name is used when he is appealed to on behalf of a sick person. As Nohochakyum has the spirits of the east to aid him, so Mensabak has for his helpers the spirits of the west.
summary.zh: 門薩巴克居於聖伊波利托附近；或即雨神。他又名尤姆卡納薩巴克——「雨雲之上的神」——凡為病者祈禱時即以此名呼之。諾霍查庫姆有東方之靈為助，門薩巴克則以西方之靈為其僚屬。

sensitivity.note: Published public-domain ethnography (1907); living ritual — describe respectfully.

passages.text: Mensabak lives near San Hipolito. He is probably identified as the god of rain. He is also called Yumkanasabak; the literal meaning would be the god, kana above, sabak the black powder — freely it is the god who is above the rain cloud. The latter name seems to be used when he is appealed to on behalf of a sick person. Just as Nohochakyum has the spirits of the east to aid him, so Mensabak has for his helpers the spirits of the west.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1907), Part II; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Year-Bearer Pages of the Dresden Codex
title.zh: 德累斯頓抄本的歲首諸頁

region.en: Dresden Codex (Yucatec tradition), symbolic pin at Uxmal, Yucatan
region.zh: 德累斯頓抄本（猶加敦傳統），以墨西哥猶加敦烏斯馬爾為象徵定位

source.work: Dresden Codex, pp. 25-28, Forstemann facsimile (1880); commentary in Schellhas (1904) and Tozzer (1941)

summary.en: Pages 25-28 of the Dresden Codex picture the four Uayeb rites that Landa describes: the year-bearer idols carried on litters, seated on the stone heaps at the four entrances of the town, each with its color, its Bacab, and its offerings. There are footprints on the idol, which Forstemann states represent the goal of a pilgrimage; the top and middle portions refer to the transportation of the idols, the bottom thirds to the feasts of the four Uayeb festivals.
summary.zh: 德累斯頓抄本25-28頁繪蘭達所述的四種瓦耶亞布祭儀：歲首神像被抬上擔架，安坐於鎮口四方的石堆之上，各具其色、其巴卡布與其祭品。神像上有足印，弗斯特曼謂其象徵朝聖之地；頁之上中二部繪神像的搬運，下三分之一繪四種瓦耶亞布祭的宴飲。

sensitivity.note: Published codex facsimile and public-domain commentary; paraphrase only.

passages.text: There is an extended discussion of the identification of idols, images, statues, and braziers in the four rituals inaugurating the years. The pages of the Dresden Codex (25-28) representing the Uayeb rites show the footprints on the idol or trunk which, Forstemann states, represent the goal of a pilgrimage; the top and middle portions refer to the transportation of the idols, whereas the bottom thirds refer to the feasts connected with the four Uayeb festivals.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1941), on Landa's New Year rituals and the Dresden pages; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: In each of the four rituals Landa gives as 'the omen of the Bacab' four names, with the four colors, the four directions, and the four Pauah Tuns; the Chacs with them are rain gods comparable to the Tlalocs. It was in these very pages that Thomas showed the rites of the Uayeb days inaugurating the new years, the codical counterpart of the colonial description.
passages.note: Condensed from Tozzer (1941) and Schellhas (1904); not verbatim throughout.
